analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run national health service providing free comprehensive health care to all residents.
analysis.headline: A bill to give every person in the United States free comprehensive health care through a new government health service was introduced by one representative, attracted zero cosponsors, never got a hearing, and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a United States Health Service — a government-run health system giving free medical, dental, mental health, drug, and long-term care to everyone in the country, paid for by new taxes on individuals and corporations and by employer contributions. It would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, private employer insurance, and veterans' health programs, and put elected community boards in charge of running hospitals and clinics. It would also have guaranteed workers paid time off for medical visits and created tuition-free training schools for health workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone living in the United States would gain free comprehensive health care with no premiums, deductibles, or bills — including the uninsured, people denied coverage for pre-existing conditions, and households paying high insurance premiums. Low-income, rural, and inner-city communities would gain new clinics and hospitals built where care is scarce. Workers would gain paid health leave (one hour per 35 hours worked), and people training for health careers would get free schooling with living stipends and childcare in exchange for a service commitment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured, underinsured, and low-income patients

how_it_helps.text: Declares every individual in the United States eligible for free health care and supplemental services — covering primary and specialized care, general hospitals, dental care, mental health, long-term care, prescription drugs, eyeglasses, and hearing aids — without charge and without discrimination based on income, health status, or any other factor.

Requires every community to run a comprehensive health center and every district a general hospital, with a regional facility for highly specialized care, and directs resources toward populations the current system leaves out — inner-city and rural areas, minorities, prisoners, and occupational groups.
Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act to give every covered employee one hour of paid health leave for every 35 hours worked, usable when the worker or a dependent needs health care.

Guarantees a detailed set of patient rights — including free choice of health workers and facilities, translated materials, informed written consent, confidentiality, dignified end-of-life care, and access to a grievance system with legal help to enforce these rights.
Puts governance in the hands of health boards elected by patients and health workers at the community level, requires open public meetings, and lets users petition to recall board members.

Creates tuition-free regional health team schools that pay students a living allowance and childcare costs, in exchange for a service commitment of at least two years working for the Service, and pays off qualifying student loans for those who join.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and corporations would pay a new income-tax surcharge, and the tax break for employer-paid health coverage would be repealed, with employer contributions to the new system funneled into a Health Service Trust Fund. Employers would also fund workplace health facilities and paid health leave. Private health insurers would lose their market, and private hospitals, clinics, and providers would lose the ability to deliver care privately through Health Service facilities — with existing health workers given hiring preference for salaried Service jobs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, corporations, and the private health industry

drawbacks.text: The financing would fall on taxpayers: a new income-tax surcharge on individuals and corporations, repeal of the deduction for medical expenses and the tax exclusion for employer health benefits, and an extra Government contribution equal to 40 percent of tax receipts flowing into the new trust fund.

Three years after services begin, the bill bars Health Service facilities from being used for private health care and bars Service employees from private practice — meaning the government system would be essentially the only way to get care, eliminating any private alternative for patients who want to pay for faster or different treatment.

The transition would be enormous: the bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee health insurance, veterans' medical programs, Indian Health Service laws, and many other health statutes, moving tens of millions of people overnight into an untested system run by newly elected local boards.

Students who accept the free health-worker training would owe the government a service commitment of at least two years, and the Service could recover damages from anyone who fails to start or finish it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain would be universal, free health care for everyone in the country — something no other bill in this Congress offered — financed by progressive taxation that replaces premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket costs. The costs are real: a substantial new tax burden on individuals and corporations, the loss of any private care option, and a high-risk transition that repeals Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans' health programs all at once in favor of untested elected boards. The bill made no effort to phase in gradually or address the transition risks in detail, which helps explain why it drew no support even from allies of national health insurance.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to six House committees, but none of them ever held a hearing or voted on it, so it quietly died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ron Dellums, a California Democrat long identified with single-payer proposals, introduced the United States Health Service Act on June 8, 1995, as the sole sponsor — no other member of the House signed on.

The bill was referred to six committees at once — Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Government Reform and Oversight, National Security, and Veterans' Affairs — meaning any progress required action by all of them.

Over the following weeks it was sent to subcommittees: Health, Government Management, Health and Environment, Military Personnel, and Hospitals and Health Care. Executive comment was requested from the Department of Defense. That was the last action ever taken.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred in any committee, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, private hospitals and providers, and employers facing the new taxes all benefited from the bill going nowhere, since the existing insurance-based system continued unchanged. Americans without affordable coverage gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and private providers; the status quo survived

for.name: Rep. Ronald V. Dellums
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alone and secured its referral to six committees; no colleague cosponsored it.

against.name: House committee chairs (104th Congress)
against.role: Chairs of the six committees of referral, all Republicans in the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in any of the six committees or their subcommittees; the bill sat for 18 months and expired.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member of either party signed on, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor was a Democrat and the House was run by Republicans who controlled the committee agenda.

industries.note: The bill voids employer obligations to provide health coverage, repeals the tax treatment that sustains employer-based insurance, repeals federal employees' health insurance, and makes free public care universally available — leaving private insurers nothing to sell. Its continuation is why the private insurance system survived unchanged.

industries.industry: Private hospitals and physicians in private practice
industries.note: Three years in, Health Service facilities could no longer be used for private care and Service employees could not practice privately, converting the delivery system to salaried public employment (with hiring preference for current health workers). Providers' fee-for-service income would end.

A national formulary would decide which drugs are covered, regional boards would buy and distribute all drugs and supplies, and the National Board could build its own manufacturing facilities — replacing a private market with a government monopsony.

Employers would owe a share of the new health tax, fund workplace health facilities, and pay accrued health leave — but would be permanently relieved of providing and administering employee health insurance.

industries.industry: Medicare and Medicaid program administrators and contractors
industries.note: The bill repeals Medicare, Medicaid, and related Social Security provisions and transfers their trust fund assets into the new Health Service Trust Fund, dissolving the existing public program infrastructure in favor of the new system.
